newsitem.title: JAPAN: Crude may hit $25 if Iraqi tension worsens - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Crude may hit $25 if Iraqi tension worsens - analyst.

text.p: Benchmark crude prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) could shoot as high as $25 per barrel later this year if the Middle East situation worsens, the director of a Japanese energy think tank said on Wednesday.
"If the tension increases, WTI (West Texas Intermediate) prices would be...$24 or $25 for some period," Tsutomu Toichi, director of the Institute of Energy Economics Japan told Reuters.
If the conflict turns out to be short-lived, NYMEX crude futures prices would be in a range of between $21 and $22 per barrel, he predicted.
WTI is a crude blend used as the benchmark for U.S. crude oil and as a reference point in pricing other grades.

The October futures contract on the ACCESS after-hours trading system jumped 30 cents to $23.65 per barrel in late-morning Asian trade following news of the second U.S. missile attack against Iraq, but then eased from the highs.
Toichi said the impact of higher crude oil prices on Japan's overall economy would be limited.
"The current import bill of oil in Japan is about 15 percent of the total import bill," he said. "Therefore, if the oil price increased 10 percent, then the impact would be just 1.5 percent."
He said an appropriate oil price range would be $15 to $20 per barrel for Dubai crude.
Unusually low oil prices are not good for Japan and other Asian countries because cheaper oil would increase those countries' dependency on Middle Eastern crude oil, Toichi said,
He also said higher oil prices would not necessarily be good for Middle Eastern oil producers.
"In the short term, higher oil prices, $20 or $25 per barrel, would be good for oil producers," he said.

"But in the longer term, they would lose their market share because non-OPEC producers would increase their production and also non-oil energy, like natural gas, coal and nuclear energy would be more economical," Toichi said.
